description: Byzantine rump state in the Peloponnese (1349–1460) that became the most culturally vibrant late Byzantine polity; Mistra served as a centre of Neoplatonic philosophy under Gemistos Plethon, whose ideas influenced Italian Renaissance humanism, while the despotate's fall to the Ottomans in 1460 marked the definitive end of Byzantine political continuity.

temporal.notes: Late Byzantine Peloponnesian territory before Ottoman conquest.

geographic.notes: Centroid approximate; polygon pending schematic or OHM sourcing.

lifecycle_phases.description: Manuel Kantakouzenos establishes Mystra as capital of the Despotate.
Palaiologos family takes over; Byzantine cultural renaissance at Mystra.
Maximum Despotate extent; Mystra is a major center of Greek learning.
Ottoman breaches of Hexamilion; fraternal civil war weakens defense.
Mehmed II conquers the Morea; last Byzantine territory extinguished.

rise_factors.description: The Hexamilion wall across the Corinth isthmus and the mountainous Peloponnese interior gave strong defensive depth.
Palaiologos family used the Morea as a base for late Byzantine cultural and political revival.
Greek Orthodox population loyalty and churchmen supported Palaiologos governance over Latin alternatives.
Established as a Byzantine appanage under the Palaiologos dynasty after 1204, the Morea became a center of Greek Orthodox cultural revival and late Byzantine learning.
The silk-producing region around Patras and Corinth generated significant revenue, supporting the court at Mystras which became a major intellectual center in the 15th century.

decline_factors.description: Ottoman campaigns under Mehmed II breached the Hexamilion 1446 and 1452; full conquest followed 1460.
Brothers Constantine and Demetrios quarreled over the Morea, dividing its defense against the Ottomans.
Albanian settlers and local archontes resisted effective central authority.
Ottoman forces under Mehmed II conquered the Morea in 1460, ending Byzantine rule eight years after the fall of Constantinople.
Bitter rivalry between the despot brothers Thomas and Demetrios Palaiologos paralyzed defensive efforts and led Demetrios to invite Ottoman intervention.
